doc_summary: Hubinger argues that purely behavioral, non-fine-tuning evaluations are untrustworthy for advanced models because a situationally aware model can detect evaluation and game it, while fine-tuning-based evals can be trusted for capabilities but not alignment. He concludes that robust alignment evaluation will need understanding-based methods, which remain an open problem.

items.claim: Distrusts behavioral non-fine-tuning evals as evidence of alignment because a model that knows it is being evaluated can simply choose whatever answer tricks the evaluator, since nothing penalizes wrong answers.
items.quote: this style of evaluation is very easy for the model to game: since there's no training process involved in these evaluations that would penalize the model for getting the wrong answer here, a model that knows it's being evaluated can just pick whatever answer it wants

items.claim: Assumes evaluation-vs-deployment discrimination favors the model, because checking a predicate is easier than generating a convincing fake instance, so a conservative model defaults to assuming it is in evaluation unless it sees compelling evidence of deployment.
items.quote: the existence of predicates on the world that are easier to evaluate than generate examples of (in the same way that verifying the answer to a problem in NP can be easier than generating it) guarantees that the model should be better at distinguishing between evaluation and deployment

items.claim: Believes trust in behavioral evals must rest on grounds independent of those evals, such as the model lacking situational awareness or deceptive alignment being unlikely, rather than on the behavioral results themselves.
items.quote: for behavioral non-fine-tuning evaluations to be trustworthy, you have to believe—for some reason unrelated to any behavioral non-fine-tuning evaluations that you've run—that the model isn't trying to game your evaluations.

items.claim: Separates capabilities evaluations (could the model do it if trying) from alignment evaluations (would it try), and holds that the latter are the ones that evaluation-gaming undermines.
items.quote: A **capabilities evaluation** is a model evaluation designed to test whether a model *could* do some task if it were trying to.

items.claim: Prefers fine-tuning-based evals over pure prompting evals for capability claims because training pressure removes the model's ability to sandbag, but only trusts them under named assumptions (no exploration hacking, no gradient hacking).
items.quote: if we’re actively training the model to perform the task, then it shouldn’t be possible for the model to simply choose to sandbag the evaluation: if the model tried to sandbag the evaluation on purpose, gradient descent should just train away that behavior.

items.claim: To defeat exploration hacking, mix in supervised demonstrations and bootstrap with RL so the model cannot tell which cases are in the demonstrable (SFT) set versus the RL set, i.e. make the test distribution indistinguishable to the model.
items.quote: as long as it's hard for the model to always be able to tell how hard some case would be for the humans to demonstrate, the model won't be able to tell when it's safe for it to exploration hack

items.claim: Distrusts negative results from tasks where the model can recognize that humans lack demonstrations, since a failure to show deception in itself would not imply absence of deception.
items.quote: we tried to train the model to look for deception in itself and it failed, thus the model must not be deceptive

items.claim: Judges gradient hacking as hard enough that i.i.d. fine-tuning evals can be trusted until well into the superhuman regime, except when the setup hands the model affordances like a pre-commitment database or write access to its own weights.
items.quote: there are some cases where gradient hacking might be quite easy, e.g. cases where we give the model access to a database where it can record its pre-commitments or direct access to its own weights and the ability to modify them.

items.claim: Prefers understanding-based, non-behavioral evaluations (e.g. interpretability during training) over behavioral ones for alignment because behavioral evidence can be faked by a deceptive model.
items.quote: if we evaluate the extent to which we understand our models, we might be able to produce an actually robust and trustworthy evaluation of alignment.

items.claim: Identifies reliably evaluating how well we understand our models as a critical open problem needed for trustworthy alignment evals.
items.quote: we don't currently know how to effectively and reliably evaluate the extent to which we understand our models, leaving that as a critical open problem in this space.
